newsitem.title: GERMANY: Allianz doesn't rule out Holocaust fund - magazine.
newsitem.headline: Allianz doesn't rule out Holocaust fund - magazine.

text.p: A top executive at Allianz AG Holding said in a magazine interview released on Saturday that the German insurance group has not yet ruled out establishing a fund to compensate victims of the Nazis.

Allianz management board member Herbert Hansmeyer told Germany's Der Spiegel magazine that Allianz was contemplating a fund similar to that established by Swiss banks even though he said the insurer lost most of its capital after World War Two.
"At the end of the war we had lost almost all of our capital and therefore our ability to take care of customers," he told Spiegel in an interview to be published on Monday.
He added, "We have not yet ruled out such a fund but it is too early to decide. We still do not know enough about our role in the Third Reich and want to make clear what happened."

Allianz has launched a major campaign to help relatives of Holocaust victims track down missing assets after it was named with six other insurers in a class-action lawsuit launched earlier this year in the United States.
The suit alleges that insurers concealed or converted the cash value and proceeds of insurance policies sold before 1946 to mainly Jewish victims of Nazi persecution.
The allegations are similar to those made against some Swiss banks alleged to have profited from the Hitler regime.
Switzerland has set up a $185 million Holocaust memorial fund with donations from banks and businesses and has proposed a $4.7 billion "Solidarity Foundation" to help victims of human rights abuses.
Hansmeyer said Allianz has shouldered some responsibility for the Nazi regime but said the Munich-based insurance group, considered one of the largest in the world, did not profit.
"It is correct that we made ourselves guilty during the Third Reich but we did not profit from the Holocaust," he said.
He confirmed to Spiegel that Allianz had insured some of the buildings at SS concentration camps and said some Allianz employees must have known what had happened in the camps.

"It is likely that some employees knew what had happened at the camps," Hansmeyer said in the interview. "But one must make a distinction between the millions who died in the gas chambers and the SS buildings. We never insured concentration camps."
